RAG access control is the part of retrieval systems that nobody demos, and document permission leaks are what appear when it is missing. The demo indexes a folder of documents, asks a question, and gets a good answer. The thing nobody checks is whether the intern who asked is allowed to see the answer, and in most first-generation builds the answer is no.

articles.description:
When you write code that sends HTTP requests to an outside server, setting a timeout is something most people remember to do. But there are three kinds of timeouts with different jobs, and a single number cannot protect against all of them.
This article walks through connect, read, and total timeouts, with results from actually running Python's requests library (2.34.0, Python 3.12.8). Some details are library-specific, but the ideas apply to other languages and HTTP clients as well.
Note: A "timeout" here means putting an upper limit on how long you wait for the other side and giving up when it is exceeded. Without one, a silent server can stall your code indefinitely.
An HTTP request roughly goes: ① connect → ② send the request → ③ receive the response. Timeouts differ by which stage the…

articles.author: Mohamed Mokbel
articles.description:
After the first cut of a talking-head video, creators still need a title, a description and a thumbnail. Language models are good at writing those. They're also good at writing them in a voice that isn't the creator's. Here's how we approached it in Cutora, and the rules that mattered more than the prompt.
Titles and descriptions are written from what the person actually said in this video. No web facts, no "industry insights". If it isn't in the transcript, it doesn't go in. That keeps the output checkable: the creator can always point to where a line came from.
The side effect is honest: if the creator said something wrong, the draft repeats it. We say so in the UI ("check it before you publish") rather than pretend the model fact-checked anything.
Early drafts described "the speaker". Nobody publishes a description of themselves in the third person. The description now has to be in the creator's own voice ("I"), and that's a check, not a style hint.
We don't generate images of people. A thumbnail idea is a moment in the video and a short phrase the creator said around that moment. "Make the picture" grabs that frame and draws the words on it, in the browser, as a PNG. The creator's face, the creator's words.
Chapters need enough material. Under a minute, or without three clear topics, the editor makes none and says why, instead of inventing "Intro / Main point / Outro" for a 28-second clip.
Everything lands in one ZIP: a README, the publish text, the thumbnail pictures, and any Shorts that exist. Nothing is posted anywhere on the creator's behalf.
Most of the work was in rules 1 and 4: stopping the model from being helpful in ways the creator didn't ask for. The prompt was the easy part.
Disclosure: I build Cutora. More on how the first cut itself is decided: https://usecutora.com/guides/how-the-first-cut-decides-what-to-remove?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=pseo&utm_campaign=publish-kit
articles.title: Generating YouTube titles and thumbnail ideas from a transcript without putting words in the creator's mouth

Kiteline is a tool for managing coding agents: Claude Code, Codex and others do the work on a computer, and you follow progress, reply and approve permissions from your phone. In practice the thing that stalls a task is rarely the model failing to write code. It is the agent stopping to wait for a person: run this command, approve this permission, pick one of these options. If you have already left the computer, those few dozen seconds turn into an hour. The last few releases (macOS 3.49.38 to 3.49.40) are mostly about exactly these moments.
Some commands need a real terminal: code signing has to reach the keychain, long jobs need someone watching the …
